```{python}
import polars as pl
import numpy as np
from lets_plot import *
import polars.selectors as cs
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

LetsPlot.setup_html(isolated_frame=True)

data_url = "https://byuidatascience.github.io/DS250-Course-Polars/Data/StarWars_with_emails.csv"
```

<!-- The first 10 rows are not part of the datset we need.

The columns headers are split across two rows. We need to clean and simplify the column headers-->

```{python}
# Read in and tidy up the first row
a = pl.Series(pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows = 10, n_rows=1, has_header=False, encoding = 'utf8-lossy').row(0))
# Note the non-aschii character in the column "Do you consider yourself to be a fan of the Expanded Universe". (column AF if you open it in Excel). 

# BTW: Detecting what it is and where can be difficult

# Lossy means that invalid utf8 values are replaced with � characters. When using other encodings than utf8 or utf8-lossy, the input is first decoded in memory with python. Defaults to utf8...ignore_errors = True does not replace the non-utf8 character with a blank space like you would hope

a[2] = "seen_any" #simply overwrite the value at index 2

# Rather than changing each column header manually,
# here we use regex to apply changes more efficiently
a = (
  a.str.replace(r".+seen.+", "seen_")
   .str.replace(r".+rank.+", "rank_")
   .str.replace(r"(.+favorably.+)", "fav_")
   .fill_null(strategy = "forward")

   .str.replace("\uFFFD+", "") #this gets rid of the question marks in a diamond characters 
   .str.strip_chars()
   .str.to_lowercase()
   .str.replace_all(" ", "_")
   .str.replace(r"location(.+)", "location")

)
a[3] = "star_wars_fan"
a[30] = "who_shot_first"
a[31] = "know_expanded_universe"
a[32] = "expanded_universe_fan"
a[33] = "star_trek_fan"
```

<!-- Combine series q and a into one series to be used as column names-->

```{python}
b = pl.Series(pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows = 11, n_rows=1, has_header=False, encoding = 'utf8-lossy').row(0))

b = (
  b.str.replace(r"Star Wars: (Episode \w+) .+", "${1}")
   .str.replace("Response", "")
   .str.replace_all(" ", "_")
   .fill_null("")
   .str.strip_chars()
)

```

```{python}
#Now combine the two series, each of which contains part of the desired column header
new_names = (a + b).to_list()

# Read in the data, skipping over the column header rows
# and use 'new_names' as the column headers
df = pl.read_csv(data_url, skip_rows=12, has_header=False, new_columns = new_names )
```

## Executive Summary

- Filtered to 835 respondents who have seen at least one Star Wars film.
- Recreated two charts from the FiveThirtyEight article to validate the dataset.
- Dropped identifying columns and one-hot encoded non-numeric columns to prepare features for the machine learning model.
- Trained a Random Forest to predict whether a respondent earns at least $50k; education and age were the strongest predictors.
- **Stretch: No**


## Methods

### Filtering to 835 Respondents

```{python}
seen_ep_cols = [c for c in df.columns if c.startswith("seen_") and c != "seen_any"]

df_filtered = df.filter(
    pl.any_horizontal([pl.col(c).is_not_null() for c in seen_ep_cols])
)

print(f"Rows after filter: {len(df_filtered)}")
```

### Article Validation

**Chart 1 — Which films have respondents seen?**

```{python}
total = len(df_filtered)

seen_data = pl.DataFrame({
    "film": ["Episode I", "Episode II", "Episode III", "Episode IV", "Episode V", "Episode VI"],
    "pct": [
        round(df_filtered[c].is_not_null().sum() / total * 100, 1)
        for c in seen_ep_cols
    ],
})

(
    ggplot(seen_data, aes(x=as_discrete("film", order_by="pct", order=1), y="pct"))
    + geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="#438CC4")
    + coord_flip()
    + scale_y_continuous(limits=[0, 100])
    + labs(title="Which Star Wars Films Have You Seen?", x="", y="% of Respondents")
    + theme_minimal()
)
```

**Chart 2 — Character favorability**

```{python}
fav_raw_cols = [c for c in df_filtered.columns if c.startswith("fav_")]

fav_summary = []
for c in fav_raw_cols:
    char = c.replace("fav_", "").replace("_", " ")
    total_familiar = df_filtered.filter(
        pl.col(c).is_not_null() & (pl.col(c) != "Unfamiliar (N/A)")
    ).height
    favorable = df_filtered.filter(
        pl.col(c).is_in(["Very favorably", "Somewhat favorably"])
    ).height
    pct = round(favorable / total_familiar * 100, 1) if total_familiar > 0 else 0
    fav_summary.append({"character": char, "pct_favorable": pct})

fav_data = pl.DataFrame(fav_summary).sort("pct_favorable", descending=True)

(
    ggplot(fav_data, aes(x=as_discrete("character", order_by="pct_favorable", order=1), y="pct_favorable"))
    + geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="#438CC4")
    + coord_flip()
    + labs(title="Character Favorability", x="", y="% Favorable")
    + theme_minimal()
)
```


### Missing Values

Missing values showed up in a few places. Respondents who didn't answer the income question got dropped since income is the target — you can't train on a row with no label. Everything else had nulls filled with the string "missing" before one-hot encoding, so the model treats no-response as its own category. Dropping income non-responses brought the dataset down from 835 to around 600 rows, which is worth keeping in mind when looking at the results.


## Results

### Classification Report

```{python}
df_pd = df_filtered.to_pandas()

# Drop identifying columns
drop_cols = [c for c in df_pd.columns if c in ["respondentid", "first_name", "last_name", "email"]]
df_pd = df_pd.drop(columns=drop_cols)

# Create target then drop income column
df_pd = df_pd.dropna(subset=["household_income"])
y = df_pd["household_income"].isin(["$50,000 - $99,999", "$100,000 - $149,999", "$150,000+"]).astype(int)
df_pd = df_pd.drop(columns=["household_income"])

# One-hot encode all non-numeric columns
cat_cols = df_pd.select_dtypes(include="object").columns.tolist()
num_cols = df_pd.select_dtypes(exclude="object").columns.tolist()

enc = OneHotEncoder(sparse_output=False, handle_unknown="ignore")
X_cat = enc.fit_transform(df_pd[cat_cols].fillna("missing"))
X_num = df_pd[num_cols].fillna(0).to_numpy()
X = np.hstack([X_num, X_cat]) if num_cols else X_cat

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)

clf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=42)
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred = clf.predict(X_test)

report = classification_report(y_test, y_pred, target_names=["< $50k", ">= $50k"], output_dict=True)
pd.DataFrame(report).T[["precision", "recall"]]
```

### Feature Importance

```{python}
all_feature_names = num_cols + enc.get_feature_names_out(cat_cols).tolist()

imp_df = pl.from_pandas(
    pd.DataFrame({"feature": all_feature_names, "importance": clf.feature_importances_})
    .sort_values("importance", ascending=False)
    .head(10)
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

(
    ggplot(imp_df, aes(x=as_discrete("feature", order_by="importance", order=1), y="importance"))
    + geom_bar(stat="identity", fill="#438CC4")
    + coord_flip()
    + labs(title="Top 10 Feature Importances", x="", y="Importance")
    + theme_minimal()
)
```

Education and age are the strongest predictors of income. Star Wars viewing habits and character favorability ratings add relatively little.


## Conclusion

The dataset lines up with the FiveThirtyEight article, and the model does confirm that education and age drive income predictions way more than anything Star Wars related. That part isn't really surprising.

The main limitation is the data itself — it's a 2014 survey of about 800 people, and after dropping rows with missing income you're working with around 600. The test set ends up being only 203 rows, which isn't a lot. The model hit 61% accuracy and the precision on the under $50k class was 0.47, basically a coin flip for that group.

For a recommendation: don't use Star Wars preferences to predict someone's income, it's not doing much. If the actual goal is predicting income, education level alone would probably get you close to the same result with something a lot simpler than a Random Forest. Future work could look at a bigger and more recent survey dataset, or try to get cleaner income data instead of the binned ranges we have here.
